newsitem.title: USA: Smith Barney to pay $1.05 mln on Espy-related suit.
newsitem.headline: Smith Barney to pay $1.05 mln on Espy-related suit.

text.p: Smith Barney Inc. agreed to pay $1.05 million to settle allegations that it slipped a 1994 Super Bowl ticket to former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy to win his influence with the Clinton administration, prosecutors said on Tuesday.
The settlement comes as independent counsel Donald Smaltz is trying to wrap up a nearly three-year-long probe of Espy for allegedly accepting favours from companies he regulated.

Espy, who has denied any wrongdoing, was notified earlier this summer that he is a target of a criminal grand jury probe and could face indictment. If indicted, he would be the highest-ranking member of the Clinton administration to face criminal charges.
The former congressman from Mississippi resigned from his cabinet post in 1994.

"Espy had a duty not to accept gifts from companies he regulates," said a source close to the investigation. "The Super Bowl ticket for the game in Atlanta was considered valuable and probably worth more than money to many people."
Smith Barney said it settled the civil lawsuit to avoid costly and protracted litigation, but insisted that it did nothing wrong.

The lawsuit, which was made public on Tuesday at the same time the settlement was announced, alleged that Smith Barney used Espy to lobby the Clinton administration on behalf of a client, Oglethorpe Power Corp.

At Smith Barney's behest, Espy approached then-Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen with a request to grant Oglethorpe a waiver of $286 million in penalties due on loans that the Georgia utility received through a U.S. Agriculture Department programme, according to prosecutors.
When that failed, Espy then went to Vice President Al Gore on two occasions to help persuade the Treasury Department to reconsider.

"That agents of a prominent securities firm would jeopardise the firm's reputation and callously disregard the law by seeking the continued assistance of the secretary of agriculture with a $2,200 gratuity is disgraceful," Smaltz said in a statement.

A New York-based managing director of Smith Barney allegedly bought a ticket for the Jan. 30, 1994 Super Bowl game from a ticket scalper for $2,200. He was placed on administrative leave with pay pending review of the situation, Smith Barney said.

"The individual banker bought tickets from a financial printer and gave them to a consultant. The consultant then gave one of them to Espy. There was no intent to influence the secretary," a spokesman for Smith Barney said. "We had no knowledge that the ticket was going to go to Espy. And Espy had no knowledge that Smith Barney paid for the ticket."
The football ticket was never used by Espy.

The lawsuit marked the first time any independent counsel has sought civil damages and penalties in a criminal investigation. Smith Barney also agreed to cooperate with Smaltz's probe as part of the settlement.
The settlement boosted to $4.5 million the amount of criminal fines, civil penalties and damages that Smaltz has won in Espy-related cases.

The probe is also investigating allegations that Espy attended a party hosted by multi-millionaire Don Tyson in 1993, and a few months later accepted tickets to watch a Dallas Cowboys football game in the Tyson Foods corporate skybox.

Although speculation has grown that indictments against Espy and Tyson Foods Inc. may soon be announced, the independent counsel's office has downplayed any sense of urgency. "We will resolve these things as completely and quickly as we can. We're not going to rush anything and we have no arbitrary time limit," said a source close to the investigation.
